chunks.title: Rods, cones & inheritance
chunks.tldr: Rods (120 million, mid-periphery) = night + peripheral vision → rod disease = night blindness + field loss. Cones (6 million, fovea) = central, colour, day → cone disease = poor VA, colour loss, photophobia.
points: Inherited retinal disease = leading cause of blind registration in UK working-age adults.
>250 genes. Genetic heterogeneity: many genes → same picture. Phenotypic heterogeneity: one gene → different pictures.
Gene testing (targeted panels) → counselling + gene therapy trials.
AD: later, milder, variable expressivity. AR / XLR: earlier, severe. XLR carrier females may show fundus signs.
XLD: very rare, lethal in boys (Aicardi). Mitochondrial: maternal only, severity depends on proportion of faulty mitochondria.
Classify: generalized (rod-cone or cone-rod) vs central (macular); stationary vs progressive.
chunks.hook: Rods = Roaming in the dark. Cones = Colour + Centre.

cards.q: Night blindness with peripheral field loss points to which photoreceptor?
Which inheritance pattern gives the mildest RP?

chunks.title: ERG basics
chunks.tldr: a-wave (negative) = photoreceptors. b-wave (positive) = bipolar + Müller cells. c-wave = RPE. Scotopic (30 min dark): rod, combined, oscillatory. Photopic (10 min light): cone, 30 Hz flicker.
points: Corneal (or lower lid skin) active electrode + forehead reference.
b-wave amplitude: a-trough to b-peak; bigger with dark adaptation.
Latency = to a-wave start. Implicit time = to b-wave peak.
Rod response: dim flash → big b, tiny a.
Combined: bright flash → big a + b.
Oscillatory potentials: inner retina, on rising b-wave.
30 Hz flicker: rods can't follow → pure cone. Critical flicker fusion ~50 Hz.
Multifocal ERG: maps function (3D 'hill of vision'). Focal ERG: macula. Pattern ERG: ganglion cells.
Uses: dystrophies, birdshot, hydroxychloroquine toxicity.
chunks.hook: a = At the receptors; b = Bipolar. Flicker 30 Hz = Cones only.

cards.q: Which ERG test isolates cone function?
cards.a: Photopic single flash and 30 Hz flicker.

chunks.title: EOG & dark adaptation
chunks.tldr: EOG = RPE + photoreceptors. Arden ratio = light peak ÷ dark trough; normal >1.85. Classic: Best disease = abnormal EOG with normal ERG. Dark adaptation: rod-cone break at 7–10 min.
points: Standing potential: cornea positive, back of eye negative.
Needs diffuse RPE disease to drop. Eye blind from disease above photoreceptors (e.g. optic nerve) → EOG normal.
Dark adaptometry: bleach rhodopsin, then measure threshold over time.
Cone branch: first 5–10 min. Rod-cone break 7–10 min. Rods fully adapted 15–30 min (100× more sensitive than cones).
Foveola test → only cone segment (no rods).
Useful for unexplained night blindness.
chunks.hook: Arden 1.85 — 'one-eighty-five or alive'. Best = Bad EOG.

cards.q: When does the rod-cone break normally occur?
cards.a: After about 7–10 minutes in the dark.

chunks.title: Retinitis pigmentosa: diagnosis
chunks.tldr: Commonest dystrophy (~1:5000), rod-cone. Triad: bone-spicule pigment, arteriolar attenuation, waxy disc pallor. Night blindness first → ring scotoma → tunnel vision. XLR worst, AD best.
points: Inheritance: sporadic, AD (often rhodopsin), AR, XLR (blind by 30s–40s).
20–30% syndromic. ~5% = Leber congenital amaurosis.
Symptoms: nyctalopia, dark adaptation difficulty, peripheral loss, photopsia; VA late.
Signs: mid-peripheral perivascular bone spicules, tessellation, macular CMO/ERM/atrophy, myopia, disc drusen.
XLR carriers: golden 'tapetal' macular reflex, patchy pigment.
Complications: PSC cataract (very common), POAG (3%), keratoconus, PVD, Coats-like reaction.
ERG: scotopic reduced early → later extinguished. EOG no light rise. DA prolonged. Fields: mid-peripheral scotomas → ring → central island.
Exclude mimics such as syphilis.
chunks.hook: RP triad = 'Bones, Bare vessels, Bland (waxy) disc'.

cards.a: Bone-spicule pigmentation, arteriolar attenuation, waxy disc pallor.

cards.q: Fundus sign in female carriers of X-linked RP?
cards.a: Golden-metallic 'tapetal' reflex at the macula (± peripheral pigment).

chunks.title: Retinitis pigmentosa: management
chunks.tldr: No cure (gene therapy in trials). Treat the treatable: cataract surgery, CMO → acetazolamide / topical CAI. Sunglasses, stop smoking, avoid retinotoxic drugs. High-dose vitamin A = marginal, risky.
points: Annual review; low vision aids, rehabilitation, social support.
Sunglasses blocking up to ~550 nm with side shields; amber indoor lenses may help contrast.
Vitamin A palmitate 15,000 IU/day: marginal; avoid in pregnancy, smokers' concerns, liver toxicity; avoid with ABCA4 mutations; monitor levels + LFTs.
Lutein (± zeaxanthin) may be safer.
Avoid/caution: sildenafil-type drugs, isotretinoin, phenothiazines, hydroxychloroquine, tamoxifen, vigabatrin.
chunks.hook: RP: fix the Cataract and the CMO — the two things you can fix.

cards.q: First-line treatment for CMO in RP?
cards.a: Oral acetazolamide or topical carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.

cards.q: In which genotype should vitamin A be avoided?

chunks.title: Syndromic RP
chunks.tldr: Usher = RP + deafness (commonest). Kearns–Sayre = CPEO + salt-and-pepper fundus (mitochondrial). Bassen–Kornzweig = acanthocytes + ataxia (fat-soluble vitamins). Refsum = phytanic acid. Bardet–Biedl = polydactyly + bull's-eye.
points: Usher (AR): ~5% of profound childhood deafness; half of deaf-blindness. Type I (75%) congenital deafness + early severe RP; type III progressive deafness.
Kearns–Sayre: ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, heart block; macular salt-and-pepper.
Abetalipoproteinaemia: failure to thrive, spinocerebellar ataxia, thorny red cells → vitamins (A, E) + low-fat diet.
Refsum: ichthyosis, neuropathy, cataract → low phytanic acid diet.
Bardet–Biedl: polydactyly, obesity, learning disability; cone-rod bull's-eye; 80% severe by 20.
chunks.hook: Treatable RP = Refsum + Bassen–Kornzweig ('diet and vitamins').

cards.q: Most common syndromic association of RP?

chunks.title: Atypical RP & Leber congenital amaurosis
chunks.tldr: Sine pigmento (no pigment), punctata albescens (white dots, progressive), sector RP (inferior, slow). LCA: blind from birth, roving eyes, flat ERG, eye-poking; RPE65 gene therapy (voretigene).
points: Retinitis punctata albescens ≈ same spectrum as fundus albipunctatus but progressive.
Sector RP: AD, inferior quadrants; may look stationary. Unilateral RP exists.
LCA: commonest genetic cause of childhood blindness; AR; ≥23 genes.
LCA signs: poor pupils, nystagmus, photophobia, normal-ish fundus early → pigment, macular coloboma-like atrophy.
Oculodigital sign: eye rubbing → enophthalmos, keratoconus.
Associations: learning disability, deafness, epilepsy, renal, skeletal.
Pigmented paravenous chorioretinal atrophy: pigment along veins, normal ERG, benign.
chunks.hook: LCA baby pokes eyes (oculodigital) — ERG flat.

cards.q: Which gene is targeted by approved LCA gene therapy?

cards.a: Constant eye poking/rubbing in blind infants (e.g. LCA).

chunks.title: Cone & cone-rod dystrophy
chunks.tldr: Young adult with falling central VA, colour loss, photophobia (not night blindness). Classic bull's-eye maculopathy. ERG: cones down, rods OK till late. FAF is key.
points: Mostly sporadic; AD and XLR too. Prognosis poor (~6/60).
Signs: normal → mottling → bull's-eye → geographic atrophy. Golden sheen in XL form.
Colour: severe deutan–tritan defect out of proportion to VA.
FAF: rings around fovea. OCT: outer retinal loss. FA not needed.
Rx: supportive, low vision aids, light protection.
chunks.hook: Cones: Can't see Colour, Can't stand light.

cards.a: Reduced photopic/flicker cone responses, rods preserved until late.

cards.q: Name three causes of bull's-eye maculopathy.
cards.a: Chloroquine/HCQ toxicity, cone dystrophy, advanced Stargardt (also Bardet–Biedl, Batten).

chunks.title: Stargardt / fundus flavimaculatus
chunks.tldr: Commonest macular dystrophy; AR ABCA4; lipofuscin in RPE. Child/teen with VA worse than fundus looks. Pisciform (fish-tail) flecks, 'beaten-bronze' macula. FA: dark choroid. Avoid vitamin A.
points: STGD1 (AR, ABCA4) commonest; STGD3/4 AD.
Once VA <6/12 → drops fast to ~6/60 and stabilises. Flecks-only = better.
May be mistaken for malingering.
Macula: mottling → 'snail slime' / beaten-bronze → GA (bull's-eye-like). CNV rare.
Flecks at RPE level; new ones appear as old ones fade.
FAF: bright flecks, dark macula, peripapillary sparing.
FA: dark (silent) choroid; fresh flecks block early, stain late.
ERG photopic normal–subnormal; EOG subnormal late.
Rx: sunglasses/blue-light protection, no vitamin A; gene/stem cell trials.
chunks.hook: Stargardt = Stars (flecks) on a Dark sky (silent choroid).

chunks.title: Flecked & crystalline retinas
chunks.tldr: Bietti: corneal + retinal crystals, East Asians, CYP4V2. Alport: perimacular dots + renal failure + deafness + anterior lenticonus (type IV collagen). Benign fleck retina: harmless.
points: Bietti (AR): young adults; crystals → choriocapillaris atrophy → diffuse chorioretinal atrophy; FA hypofluorescent patches. No treatment.
Alport (mostly XLR): flecks subtle, ERG normal, vision excellent; anterior lenticonus, PPMD.
Familial benign fleck retina (AR): flecks to periphery sparing fovea, normal ERG.
Other crystals: Sjögren–Larsson (macula, ichthyosis), gyrate atrophy, MacTel 2, tamoxifen, canthaxanthine.
chunks.hook: Alport: Ears, Eyes, Kidneys ('can't pee, can't hear, can't see well up close' – lenticonus).

cards.q: Crystals in cornea and retina, East Asian patient?

chunks.title: CSNB & achromatopsia
chunks.tldr: CSNB: night blind from infancy, non-progressive. Normal fundus (complete/incomplete) or abnormal: Oguchi (golden fundus that normalises in dark = Mizuo) and fundus albipunctatus. Rod monochromat: 6/60, nystagmus, photophobia, no colour.
points: CSNB type 1 complete: no rod pathway, cones OK. Type 2 incomplete: both affected.
AR/XLR CSNB often myopia + nystagmus + poor VA.
Oguchi (AR): golden sheen in light → normal after long dark adaptation.
Fundus albipunctatus: tiny white dots, fovea spared, RLBP1; stationary (vs punctata albescens).
Achromatopsia: CNGB3 (~50%), CNGA3 (~25%); gene therapy promising.
Rod monochromatism (AR): VA ~6/60, nystagmus, photophobia, no colour, abnormal photopic ERG.
Blue cone monochromatism (XLR): VA 6/6–6/9, no colour, no nystagmus.
chunks.hook: Oguchi = Gold that fades in the dark (Mizuo).

cards.a: Golden fundus sheen in light that disappears after prolonged dark adaptation (Oguchi disease).

cards.q: Rod monochromatism – VA and key features?
cards.a: ~6/60, congenital nystagmus, photophobia, total colour blindness.

chunks.title: Best vitelliform dystrophy
chunks.tldr: AD, BEST1 (bestrophin, RPE ion channel). 'Egg yolk' macular lesion in childhood. EOG very abnormal (Arden <1.5) even in carriers; ERG normal.
points: 2nd commonest macular dystrophy.
Stages: pre-vitelliform (abnormal EOG only) → vitelliform (yolk, good VA) → pseudohypopyon (often puberty) → vitelliruptive ('scrambled egg', VA drops) → atrophic.
Vision fair until middle age; loss from CNV, scar, GA.
FAF: very bright yolk. FA: blocks. OCT: material under/in RPE.
Multifocal vitelliform lesions in adults with normal EOG ≠ Best.
chunks.hook: Best = Bad EOG, fine ERG. Egg: sunny side up → settles (pseudohypopyon) → scrambled.

cards.q: Diagnostic test in Best disease, abnormal even in carriers?

chunks.title: Adult vitelliform & pattern dystrophies
chunks.tldr: Adult-onset vitelliform: small yellow subfoveal blob in older adults, normal EOG, PRPH2 often. Pattern dystrophies (PRPH2): butterfly, reticular, spider (macroreticular), Stargardt-like — mild vision effects.
points: Adult vitelliform: smaller than Best; mild VA drop; may become CNV or atrophy. FA: dark centre + bright ring.
Vitelliform look also from basal laminar drusen, VMT, pseudodrusen.
Butterfly: yellow/pigment spokes at fovea.
Reticular (Sjögren): pigment network ('fishnet').
Multifocal pattern mimicking flavimaculatus but choroid not dark.
Macroreticular (spider); fundus pulverulentus (very rare).
chunks.hook: PRPH2 = 'Pattern Pretty Harmless'.

cards.q: How to distinguish multifocal pattern dystrophy from Stargardt on FA?
cards.a: Pattern dystrophy lacks the dark choroid.

chunks.title: Drusen dystrophies: North Carolina, Doyne, Sorsby
chunks.tldr: North Carolina: AD, non-progressive, grades 1–3 (drusen → confluent → coloboma-like). Doyne honeycomb (EFEMP1): radial drusen incl. nasal to disc, young. Sorsby (TIMP3): drusen + CNV in 40s + nyctalopia.
points: North Carolina: complete penetrance, variable expression; grade 2 risk CNV.
Doyne / malattia leventinese: early AMD-like; symptoms 40–50s; EOG subnormal late.
Sorsby: think when a young adult has drusen + CNV; peripheral atrophy by 70s.
Progressive bifocal chorioretinal atrophy: atrophy temporal + nasal to disc; nystagmus, myopia, RD.
chunks.hook: Sorsby = Sorry, CNV at 40. Doyne = Drusen like Daisy petals (radial).

cards.q: Radially orientated drusen extending nasal to the disc in a young adult?

chunks.title: Other macular dystrophies
chunks.tldr: Quick list: concentric annular (bull's-eye, good prognosis), central areolar choroidal (central GA, poor), dominant CMO (teenagers, no leak response), Sjögren–Larsson (macular crystals + ichthyosis), MIDD (mitochondrial diabetes + deafness, macular atrophy).
points: Benign concentric annular: AD, ring scotoma, FA annular window.
Central areolar choroidal dystrophy: AD, 30–40s, well-defined central atrophy with large choroidal vessels.
Dominant CMO: untreatable → GA.
Sjögren–Larsson (AR): fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase; glistening crystals by age 2; spastic diplegia.
Familial ILM dystrophy: glistening surface, poor prognosis.
MIDD: ~1% of diabetes; macular dystrophy but vision usually OK.
chunks.hook: Crystals + scaly skin in a toddler → Sjögren–Larsson.

cards.q: Maternally inherited diabetes and deafness – macular finding?
cards.a: Progressive pattern-like macular atrophy/pigment change, vision usually preserved.

chunks.title: Choroideremia
chunks.tldr: XLR (CHM gene): boys with night blindness → choroid + RPE vanish, leaving bare sclera; fovea spared till late. Carriers: patchy peripheral mottling. Gene therapy in trials.
points: Carrier mum: 50% sons affected, 50% daughters carriers.
Early: RP-like mid-peripheral RPE change; later scalloped atrophy spreading.
End-stage: few large choroidal vessels on white sclera, optic atrophy.
FAF: speckled with foveal island. FA/ICGA: choriocapillaris absent, large vessels remain.
ERG: scotopic absent, photopic severely reduced.
Useful vision usually until ~50s–60s.
chunks.hook: Chorio-remia = choroid's remains gone → white sclera.

cards.a: Bare sclera with a few large choroidal vessels, foveal island spared until late.

chunks.title: Gyrate atrophy
chunks.tldr: AR, ornithine aminotransferase (OAT) deficiency → high ornithine. Scalloped 'gyrate' patches of atrophy merging from periphery. Myopia + nyctalopia. Rx: vitamin B6 + arginine-restricted diet.
points: Teens: myopia, night blindness.
Sharply defined round/oval atrophic patches; crystals at posterior pole; fovea spared till late.
Early cataract, vitreous degeneration, CMO, ERM.
Confirm: serum ornithine.
B6-responsive type is milder.
Legal blindness ~50 yrs.
chunks.hook: Gyrate = Ornithine Overload → cut Arginine, add B6.

chunks.title: X-linked juvenile retinoschisis
chunks.tldr: Boys 5–10 yrs, poor reading. Spoke-wheel foveal schisis (all), peripheral schisis inferotemporal (50%). Split is in the NFL (vs OPL in senile). ERG: electronegative (b < a). Rx: topical/oral CAI.
points: Gene RS1; Müller cell defect.
Peripheral inner leaf holes → 'vitreous veils'; silvery dendritic figures.
Complications: vitreous/schisis haemorrhage, RD, NV.
OCT: cysts INL/OPL. FA: no leakage (unlike CMO).
ERG: selective b-wave reduction if peripheral schisis.
Dorzolamide may thin fovea. Don't operate just to flatten schisis (non-progressive).
chunks.hook: Bicycle-wheel fovea in a boy → XLRS; CMO that doesn't leak.

cards.a: Electronegative ERG – b-wave reduced more than a-wave.

cards.q: At which layer does juvenile retinoschisis split?
cards.a: Nerve fibre layer (vs outer plexiform in acquired senile retinoschisis).

chunks.title: Stickler & Wagner
chunks.tldr: Stickler: commonest inherited cause of childhood RD (~50% in 1st decade, giant tears). High myopia, optically empty vitreous, cataract + Pierre Robin face, joint hypermobility, deafness. Wagner: same eye picture, no systemic features.
points: STL1 COL2A1 (membranous vitreous, commonest); STL2 COL11A1 (beaded vitreous, deafness); STL3 COL11A2 (no eye signs).
Systemic: flat midface, micrognathia, cleft palate, bifid uvula, early arthritis.
Eye: retrolental membrane, equatorial membranes, radial lattice, wedge/fleck cataract, glaucoma (angle anomaly), rarely ectopia lentis.
Rx: prophylactic 360° laser/cryo; RD repair often vitrectomy, PVR common.
Wagner (AD, VCAN): low myopia, empty vitreous, avascular strands, progressive chorioretinal atrophy, nyctalopia; RD in up to 50%; no broad prophylaxis.
Kniest: COL2A1, short stature, round face.
chunks.hook: Stickler = Sticks to whole body (face, joints, ears). Wagner = Wagging only eyes.

cards.q: Most common inherited cause of retinal detachment in children?

chunks.title: FEVR & other vitreoretinopathies
chunks.tldr: FEVR = 'ROP without prematurity': avascular temporal periphery, straightened vessels, dragged disc/macula. Screen relatives; wide-field FA; laser avascular retina. Enhanced S-cone: night blind + nummular pigment + schisis (NR2E3).
points: FEVR: AD mostly; stages 1 avascular → 2 NV ± exudate → 3 macula-sparing RD → 4 macula-on RD → 5 total.
FEVR: lifelong follow-up; anti-VEGF temporizing; vitrectomy for RD.
Enhanced S-cone / Goldmann–Favre (AR): too many blue cones; cystoid maculopathy without leakage.
Snowflake degeneration (AD, KCNJ13): white-without-pressure → snowflakes → sheathing → atrophy; good prognosis.
ADNIV (CAPN5): panuveitis, NV, TRD; selective b-wave loss.
ADVIRC (BEST1): circumferential pigment band between ora and equator; nanophthalmos; good prognosis.
chunks.hook: FEVR = ROP in a full-term baby (check family).

cards.a: Wide-field fluorescein angiography (shows peripheral avascularity and leakage).

chunks.title: Albinism
chunks.tldr: Low melanin → foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus, iris transillumination, pale fundus, too many fibres cross at the chiasm (VEP). Tyrosinase-negative = white hair, VA <6/60. Ocular albinism = XLR.
points: Hair-bulb incubation test (reliable after age 5).
Skin cancer risk (BCC/SCC) → sun protection.
Tyrosinase-negative OCA (AR): no melanin ever; pink-eyed; pendular nystagmus (improves with age).
Tyrosinase-positive OCA: some melanin, darkens with age.
Also: high refractive error, positive angle kappa, squint, no stereopsis.
Chediak–Higashi: infections. Hermansky–Pudlak: bleeding + pulmonary fibrosis. Waardenburg (AD): white forelock, heterochromia, telecanthus, deafness.
Ocular albinism carriers: iris translucency, mud-splattered fundus.
chunks.hook: Albino = Pale, Pendular, Pitless fovea, Pathway crosses too much.

cards.a: Excess crossing of fibres – most fibres decussate (shown by asymmetric VEP).

chunks.title: Cherry-red spot
chunks.tldr: Retina around the fovea goes white/opaque; thin fovea still shows red choroid. Causes: CRAO, storage diseases (Tay–Sachs, Sandhoff, Niemann–Pick A/B, GM1, sialidosis, Farber), toxins, commotio retinae.
points: Storage diseases: mostly AR; spot fades as RNFL dies → optic atrophy.
GM1: death by ~2 yrs, corneal haze. Sialidosis: myoclonus.
Niemann–Pick: A and B have spot; C has gaze palsy.
Farber: hoarse voice, nodules, joint pain.
Toxins: quinine, dapsone, gentamicin, CO, methanol.
chunks.hook: White retina, red bullseye → artery blocked or neurons stuffed with lipid.

cards.q: Two lipid storage diseases with a cherry-red spot?
cards.a: Tay–Sachs and Niemann–Pick (also Sandhoff, GM1, sialidosis, Farber).
